newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: GUATEMALA CATTLEMEN DEMAND GOVERNMENT SUPPORT.
newsitem.headline: GUATEMALA CATTLEMEN DEMAND GOVERNMENT SUPPORT.

text.p: Guatemala's cattlemen, faced with slumping exports and dwindling herds, are demanding more government support for the beef business, an industry spokesman said on Monday.

At a recent forum on strategies, cattlemen drafted a petition which asked for new laws to support the industry, a new cattle census, and help to fighting Mexico's high import tariffs, Roberto Herman, manager of the Southwest Guatemala Cattle Association (AGSOGUA), told Reuters.

Experts say Guatemalan cattle stocks have shrunk -- from four million head to about half that -- since the 1980s. Also, beef exports are also in a slump due to low international prices and profitable crops taking over ranching land.
Herman said another huge problem for ranchers is that landless peasants frequently invade cattle ranches to set up houses and plant crops.
Land invasions are illegal, but Herman said the law is unenforcable unless the government promises to protect judges and witnesses and makes protection of private property a priority.
Herman said beef producers also asked for the government to help them fight illegal cattle crossing from Honduras.

Guatemala could lose its certification as a zone free of certain cattle diseases since there are no controls at the border to guarantee that the Honduran cattle comes in free of those diseases, according to Herman.

Beef producers are also asking for Guatemala to fight for lower Mexican tariffs on beef. Tariffs are currently part of ongoing free trade negotiations between Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras (known as the Northern Triangle) and Mexico.
Mexico currently has 15 percent tariffs for live cattle, 20 percent for fresh meat and 25 percent for frozen meat.

Herman admitted that in order to negotiate with Mexico the Northern Triangle countries must to unify their own regulations on duties and sanitary requirements for beef traded between their own markets.

The last official cattle census here was in 1979 and the industry desperately needs an accurate accounting of how many head of cattle the country has, in order to plan for internal consumption and exports, Herman said.
"We've asked the president that he commits himself to a new census," he said.
